title: Mixed Graph (Bar + Line) DI
tagline: Year 3 — A bar chart and a line chart on one set of axes: reading both and combining them

introduction.overview: A mixed graph shows two kinds of data together, usually bars for an absolute quantity (such as revenue) and a line for a rate (such as profit percentage). The two are linked: the rate applies to the quantity, so multiplying them gives a new quantity (profit). The skill is to read each series on its own scale and then combine them correctly.
introduction.placementRelevance: Bar-plus-line graphs are the standard "hard" graph in DI sections of company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Company dashboards plot revenue as bars and margins as a line, and managers read profit from both.

learningObjectives: Read the bar series and the line series on their own scales
Combine rate and amount to get new quantities
Find years of highest growth and highest margin
Avoid mixing percentage points and percentages

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Profit = revenue × profit % ÷ 100. Expenses = revenue − profit. Percentage change = change ÷ old × 100.

coreDefinitions: Primary axis: the scale that the bars use.
Secondary axis: the scale that the line uses (here percentage).
Derived series: a series you compute from two given series.
Margin: profit as a percentage of revenue.
Percentage point: the arithmetic difference between two percentages.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: The bars say how big, the line says how profitable. Multiply them to learn how much profit.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Write a six-row table from the graph: year, revenue, margin, then add profit and expenses columns. Every question is then a lookup.

mainNarrative: Table: 2018 revenue 125 at 8% profit gives 10; 2019 150 at 12% gives 18; 2020 180 at 15% gives 27; 2021 160 at 10% gives 16; 2022 200 at 16% gives 32; 2023 240 at 20% gives 48 (₹ crore).
Growth: profit rose from 32 to 48 between 2022 and 2023, which is 16 ÷ 32 = 50%. Revenue rose from 125 to 240 between 2018 and 2023: 115 ÷ 125 = 92%.
Be careful with margins: a rise in margin from 16% to 20% is 4 percentage points but 25% in percentage terms.
A high margin does not mean high profit. The highest profit is in 2023 (48) because both revenue and margin are highest.

deepDiveAspects.title: Percentage points
deepDiveAspects.content: Margin change is best stated in percentage points; profit change in percent.

deepDiveAspects.title: Ratio of revenue to expenses
deepDiveAspects.content: Revenue ÷ expenses is greater than 1 whenever there is a profit.

solvedExamples.title: Derive profit
solvedExamples.question: Revenue in 2021 was ₹160 crore and the profit margin was 10%. What was the profit?
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: The margin is a rate on revenue.

solvedExamples.title: Expenses
solvedExamples.question: In 2023, revenue was ₹240 crore and profit was ₹48 crore. What were the expenses?

solvedExamples.title: Growth
solvedExamples.question: Profit rose from ₹32 crore (2022) to ₹48 crore (2023). By what percentage?

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Add profit and expense columns once; then every question is a single lookup or a simple ratio.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the line on the bar scale
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Note which axis each series uses.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Profit must be less than revenue.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Write the six-row table with all derived columns.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: High margin does not mean high profit.

easy.question:
Mixed graph data. The bars show revenue (₹ crore) and the line shows profit as a percentage of revenue.

Year | Revenue (₹ crore) | Profit (% of revenue)
2018 | 125 | 8%
2019 | 150 | 12%
2020 | 180 | 15%
2021 | 160 | 10%
2022 | 200 | 16%
2023 | 240 | 20%

What was the revenue in 2020 (₹ crore)?
easy.explanation: The bar for 2020 shows ₹180 crore. The answer is 180.

advanced.explanation: Expenses ÷ revenue = 100% − margin, which is lowest when the margin is highest (20% in 2023). Answer: 2023.
